T1: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing-protection products for specific use cases because they value specialized performance and aesthetics for those activities. Who benefits: End‑users (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, outdoor enthusiasts) gain better hearing protection tailored to their unique needs.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is designed to meet specific activity demands (e.g., sound transmission for concerts, noise reduction for industrial work, comfort for outdoor activities), users are willing to pay a premium and adopt dedicated devices.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering distinct product lines (e.g., musician headphones, industrial earmuffs) at premium prices, leveraging its existing R&D and brand reputation, and potentially expanding direct‑to‑consumer sales.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for specialized hearing protection.; Hellberg can design and market products differentiated for each use case.; The market for specialized hearing protection is large enough to justify a separate line.. Predictions: Surveyed users will express higher intent to purchase a specialized product compared to a generic hearing protector.; Sales of Hellberg products in targeted use cases will grow faster than overall market growth..

T2: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing-protection products because they already own multiple pairs and seek to minimize hassle and cost. Who benefits: Consumers benefit by owning a single solution for multiple use cases, reducing the need to buy multiple devices.. Why behaviour changes: When a product can serve multiple activities (e.g., home, office, outdoor), users are motivated to switch to a single device to avoid owning and managing multiple pairs.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering versatile, multi‑purpose hearing protectors at competitive prices, leveraging its existing brand for multiple‑device adoption, and potentially expanding to direct‑to‑consumer channels.. Assumptions: Consumers are already owning multiple hearing devices for different activities.; A single, versatile product can be marketed effectively as a cost‑saving solution.; The market for multi‑purpose hearing protection is large enough to justify a separate line.. Predictions: Surveyed users will report owning multiple hearing devices for different uses.; Willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose device will be higher than for a generic single‑purpose product..

Test "Consumer Choice Test: Specialized vs Multi-Use Hearing Protection" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 300 adult consumers (150 per group) via a panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two product descriptions: (A) a specialized hearing protector designed for a single use case (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, hunters) with price €120; (B) a multi-use hearing protector marketed as suitable for multiple activities (home, office, outdoor) with price €100. Both descriptions include the same basic safety features and brand reputation. Participants are asked to indicate their intent to purchase (1‑10 scale) and the maximum price they would pay. The test also collects demographic data (age, occupation, previous hearing‑protection ownership).. Sample: 300 adult consumers (150 per group) recruited via an online panel to match the target demographic of Hellberg’s existing customer base.. Measure: Primary outcome: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each product description. Secondary outcome: maximum price willing to pay (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Group A (specialized product) will have a higher average purchase intent and maximum price than Group B (multi‑use product).; T2: Group B (multi‑use product) will have a higher average purchase intent and maximum price than Group A (specialized product).. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than for Group B, conclude T1 is better supported. If the average purchase intent for Group B is at least 1.5 points higher than for Group A, conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the evidence is inconclusive and the test does not resolve the theories.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Home-Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 300 home-studio creators (defined as individuals using microphones for personal content creation, not professionals). Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: Condition A) Product description emphasizing high-quality audio performance and professional-grade credentials; Condition B) Product description emphasizing brand differentiation and professional status. In both conditions, the product is priced at a price point comparable to other mid-range studio mics (e.g., €500). Participants are asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale (1‑2‑3‑4‑5‑6‑7) and their likelihood to purchase (on a 7-point scale).. Sample: 300 home-studio creators (estimated from sources suggesting a growing home-studio segment). Measure: WTP and purchase likelihood for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will yield higher average WTP and purchase likelihood because creators value high-quality audio and are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade tools.; T2: Condition B will yield higher average WTP and purchase likelihood because creators seek brand differentiation and professional status, and are willing to pay more for a brand-associated product.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in Condition A is at least 1.5 points higher than in Condition B, conclude T1 is more likely. If Condition B is at least 1.5 points higher, conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the evidence is inconclusive.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Who benefits: Consumers seeking stylish and comfortable hearing protection for recreational activities; Hellberg Safety benefits from higher margins and brand extension.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with style and comfort, not just necessity.; There is sufficient market space for a fashion-focused hearing‑protection category.; Hellberg can design and market products that meet these lifestyle expectations.. sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.

Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.

T1: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they need a reliable, durable machine for routine yard work, and Deere can capture value by offering a high‑quality product through its existing dealer network. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small‑holder farmers who need a functional, long‑lasting tractor for lawn and garden tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently rely on generic lawn mowers or other brands; they will switch to Deere if they perceive Deere as a trusted, durable brand that is readily available through existing dealers.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors directly to dealers, who then sell to consumers, earning a margin on each unit and building brand loyalty that can support future sales.. Assumptions: Deere’s existing dealer network can reach individual buyers effectively.; Consumers value durability and reliability over price.; Deere can produce tractors at a cost that allows a dealer margin.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn and garden tractor, dealers will report increased sales of that model compared to other brands.; Consumer surveys will show higher brand trust for Deere among lawn and garden tractor owners.; Deere’s market share in lawn and garden tractors will increase in regions where dealers are active..

T2: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are willing to pay a premium for a brand that offers a superior user experience, such as comfort, ease of use, and innovative features, and Deere can capture value by positioning its tractors as premium products through its existing dealer network. Who benefits: Individual homeowners who value a comfortable, efficient, and modern lawn care experience and are willing to pay more for it.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use older, less comfortable equipment; they will switch to Deere if they perceive Deere as offering a superior user experience that justifies the higher price.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors directly to dealers, who then sell to consumers at a premium, earning higher margins and building brand loyalty that can support future sales of higher‑priced models.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for comfort and ease of use.; Deere can design tractors with features that meet this premium demand.; Dealers are willing to stock and promote premium models.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a premium lawn and garden tractor, dealers will report higher average selling prices compared to standard models.; Consumer surveys will show higher willingness to pay for comfort and ease of use.; Deere’s market share in premium lawn and garden tractors will increase in regions where dealers are active..

Test "Deere Dealer Survey on Consumer Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey of 200 individual homeowners and small‑holder farmers in the United States, recruited via a panel. Participants are asked about their current lawn and garden equipment (brand, model, age), their willingness to pay for a premium lawn and garden tractor, and their interest in a differentiated consumer proposition from Deere (e.g., a model with enhanced comfort, ease of use, or additional features). The survey also asks about their primary purchase criteria (e.g., durability, price, brand trust).. Sample: 200 participants, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region to reflect the target market.. Measure: Primary outcome: binary choice between "Would purchase a differentiated Deere consumer lawn and garden tractor" (Yes/No). Secondary outcomes: (a) average willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars for a premium model; (b) perceived importance of comfort/ease of use (1‑5 scale).. Predictions: T1: Participants will choose "Would purchase" at a rate ≥ 50% because they need a reliable, durable machine for routine yard work and trust Deere’s brand through dealers.; T2: Participants will choose "Would purchase" at a rate ≥ 50% because they value a premium user experience (comfort, ease of use) and are willing to pay a higher price for it, even if the dealer network is unchanged.. Decision rule: If the purchase rate for the differentiated proposition is ≥ 50% and the average WTP for the premium model is ≥ $500, then the evidence supports T2 (premium demand). If the purchase rate is ≤ 40% or the average WTP is ≤ $300, then the evidence supports T1 (durability‑driven demand). If neither condition is met, the evidence is inconclusive.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey (X1) to test demand for a premium model versus demand for durability/reliability. If the survey shows a purchase rate ≥50% and average willingness to pay ≥$500, proceed to develop a premium model; otherwise, focus on existing dealer network and existing product lines. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey (X1) to test demand for a premium model versus demand for durability/reliability. If the survey shows a purchase rate ≥50% and average willingness to pay ≥$500, proceed to develop a premium model; otherwise, focus on existing dealer network and existing product lines. Target customer: Individual homeowners and small‑holder farmers who need a reliable, durable machine for routine yard work.. Value proposition: A lawn and garden tractor that offers superior durability, reliability, and brand trust through the existing dealer network, leveraging Deere’s existing manufacturing and distribution capabilities.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 200‑participant survey (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated model.. Uncertainty: Demand for a premium model versus demand for durability/reliability is uncertain; the survey will resolve this.. Would change if: If the survey shows a purchase rate <40% or average willingness to pay <$300, the evidence would support T1 and we would recommend focusing on durability‑driven demand.; If the survey shows a purchase rate ≥50% and average willingness to pay ≥$500, the evidence would support T2 and we would recommend investing in a premium model.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a hearing protector with a unique design compared to a standard model.; Sales of limited-edition or personalized products will outpace standard models in a controlled test.; Direct-to-consumer sales will generate higher average order value than through retailers..

Who benefits: Safety-conscious consumers and industrial buyers who require certified, high-performance hearing protection.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is promoted as meeting or exceeding regulatory standards, consumers trust it more and are willing to pay a premium for assurance of safety and compliance.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by emphasizing certification, offering compliance-focused marketing, and selling through industrial channels where safety is paramount, potentially commanding higher margins.. Assumptions: Regulatory compliance is a primary purchase criterion for a significant segment of consumers.; Certification signals can be effectively communicated to end‑users.; Industrial buyers prioritize safety over price when selecting hearing protection.. Predictions: Surveyed industrial buyers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for a hearing protector with visible certification compared to a non‑certified model.; Sales of compliance‑focused products will be higher in regions with stringent safety regulations.; Partnerships with safety‑focused retailers will increase sales among industrial customers..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Customized vs. Safety-First Hearing Protection" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Both concepts are described as high-quality, comfortable, and marketed to the same demographic. Respondents are asked to indicate the maximum price they would pay for each concept (EUR).. Sample: 300 respondents (150 per segment). Measure: Maximum price willingness-to-pay (EUR) for each concept.. Predictions: T1: Respondents assigned to the customized concept will report a willingness-to-pay at least 20% higher than those assigned to the safety-first concept.; T2: Respondents assigned to the safety-first concept will report a willingness-to-pay at least 15% higher than those assigned to the customized concept.. Decision rule: Calculate the average willingness-to-pay for each concept. If the average willingness-to-pay for the customized concept exceeds the safety-first concept by at least 10% (e.g., 20% vs. 10%), conclude that T1 is better supported. (binary: Yes/No).. Sample: 300 respondents (150 per group). Measure: Purchase intent (binary: Yes/No) for each product variant.. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the differentiated version will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for the generic version.; T2: Purchase intent for the differentiated version will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for the generic version.. Homeownership of one-family detached homes rose significantly in the 1950s, modestly in the 1960s and 1970s, dropped slightly in the 1980s, and shows an extremely small increased in the 1990s, reaching 87 percent in 2000 (see graph).

An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
International Harvester introduced the Cub Cadet in 1961; Wheel Horse, Bolens, and Simplicity, to mention a few, were also dominate players before John Deere came onto the scene.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.

T1: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it offers a unique, customizable experience that aligns with personal style or activity, creating demand for premium pricing. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking distinctive, comfortable hearing protection that reflects their identity or lifestyle.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is marketed as a fashion accessory or activity-specific solution, consumers are willing to pay more for a product that signals their values and interests.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering limited-edition designs, personalization options, and higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales, leveraging its design expertise to create a differentiated brand.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for hearing protection that is not just functional but also expressive.; Marketing can effectively communicate the product’s unique design and activity-specific benefits to target segments.; Distribution channels can be adapted to reach these consumers (e.g., online fashion platforms, specialty retailers).. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for a hearing protector with a unique design compared to standard models.; Sales of limited-edition or personalized products will show higher unit margins compared to standard product lines.; Social media engagement (likes, shares) for design-focused campaigns will be at least 20% higher than for standard product launches..

T2: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is marketed as a safety-first product that complies with stringent regulations, creating demand for high-quality, reliable protection that is perceived as a professional choice. Who benefits: Safety-conscious consumers, industrial buyers, and regulatory bodies seeking to meet compliance standards.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is positioned as a regulatory-grade solution, consumers trust it as a safe choice, and industrial buyers prioritize compliance, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for certified products.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by emphasizing certification, offering compliance-focused marketing, and selling through industrial channels, leveraging its existing R&D and production capabilities to meet regulatory requirements.. Assumptions: Regulatory compliance is a primary purchase criterion for safety-critical products.; Consumers and buyers trust certification as a signal of safety.; Marketing can effectively communicate compliance benefits to target segments.. Predictions: Surveyed industrial buyers will indicate willingness to pay at least 10% more for a hearing protector with a visible compliance certification.; Sales of compliance-focused products will show higher unit margins compared to standard product lines.; Compliance-focused marketing will generate higher lead conversion rates among safety-focused segments..

Assumptions: Small‑garden ownership and homeownership rates in 1962 are sufficient to create a sizable consumer market.; Consumers value affordability and ease of maintenance over premium features.; Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor at a price point that attracts individual buyers.. T2: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are a status symbol and a symbol of home ownership, creating a market demand that Deere can capture by offering a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes brand prestige. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and demonstrate property ownership.. Why behaviour changes: Post‑World War II suburban growth and rising homeownership increase the number of households seeking products that signal affluence and community status.. How value is captured: Deere can price consumer tractors at a premium, leveraging its existing brand reputation and dealer network to sell directly to consumers, capturing higher margins.. Assumptions: Homeownership rates in 1962 are high enough to create a sizable market for status‑driven purchases.; Consumers associate Deere with quality and prestige, making it a desirable brand for status signaling.; Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor that maintains brand prestige while being affordable for middle‑income households.. Predictions: Sales of lawn and garden tractors will be concentrated in suburban and urban markets with high homeownership.; Deere will capture a share of the consumer market that is proportional to its brand prestige and dealer network presence.; Consumer demand will be driven by the desire to show off ownership and status rather than purely functional need..
